newsitem.title: USA: IMP sued again by holders alleging insider trading.
newsitem.headline: IMP sued again by holders alleging insider trading.

text.p: A new group of IMP Inc shareholders have filed a class action suit against the company and four of its officers alleging they sold their stock at "artificially inflated prices", while they misled investors into buying.

In papers filed in the U.S. District Court in Delaware, the plaintiffs claim the defendants, IMP Chief Executive Barry Carrington, chief financial officer Charles Isherwood, former senior vice president David Laws, controller George Rassam, together with three other officers, sold about 1.2 million shares of IMP in May at an average price of $20 a share, or about $23.6 million.

The stock previously traded between $6-$8, despite five years of increasing revenues. It began to rise in April after CNBC correspondent Dan Dorfman gave a "positive report" and Kaufman Brothers' analyst A.A. LaFountain repeated a buy rating following conversations with IMP management.

The plaintiffs, seven individuals and FCC Products Inc, say they paid about $809,000 to buy 51,000 shares at $15 to $16 a share between April 24 and July 22 after IMP told analysts and investors on May 1 that the company "was enjoying strong demand for its products, its backlog was strong and growing and IMP expected to (achieve) earnings per share of at least $.40," court papers say.
According to the lawsuit, the defendants "put this false information into the market to support and inflate IMP's stock price (and) they commenced a massive insider bailout beginning on May 3".
The stock peaked at $23 1/2 per share on May 7 then dropped to $5 7/8 on July 23 when IMP said it would fire 23 percent of its workforce because of a "softening market".

IMP, of San Jose, California, is the inventor of the Electronically Programmable Analog Circuit and a major supplier of analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits for computer, communications and control applications.
The plaintiffs seek unspecified compensatory damages against the defendants for alleged violation of the Securities and Exchange Commission law requiring full disclosure.
A company spokesman told Reuters the Delaware lawsuit and similar ones filed earlier in San Diego and San Jose California "are frivolous and the company will fight them vigorously".
